title: Selenium, Toxic Metals and Megadose Vitamins: Keshan, Chromium VI, Manganism, Hip Cobalt, Biotin, B6 and Vitamin A
summary: Learn the narrow selenium window from Keshan cardiomyopathy to selenosis, the classic injuries from hexavalent chromium, manganese and hip-implant cobalt, and how megadose biotin, pyridoxine and vitamin A cause harm or distort immunoassays.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 27 Hits 9 (selenium deficiency: Keshan disease, skeletal myopathy; selenosis signs), 11 (chromium VI carcinogen, manganism, hip-implant cobalt toxicity) and 14 (biotin immunoassay interference, high-dose B6 neuropathy, vitamin A teratogenicity). Checked against Shimada 2021, Genchi 2023, Rederstorff 2006, Morris 2013, Shin 2023, Kwakye 2015, Crutsen 2022, Luong 2020, Hadtstein 2021 and Carazo 2021 (all full text via Europe PMC). Nuances: B6 neuropathy is not confined to doses above 100 mg/day, since EFSA sets the upper limit at 25 mg/day and cases are reported near or below it (rv-b6-neuropathy-dose-threshold); prosthetic hip cobalt toxicity also follows revision of fractured ceramic bearings to a metal head, not only metal-on-metal bearings (rv-cobalt-hip-revised-ceramic); manganism mimics but is distinguishable from Parkinson disease (rv-manganism-distinguishable-pd); holding biotin needs a dose-dependent washout and the error direction depends on assay format (rv-biotin-washout-direction-ch27). Not taught (pending): selenium toxicity at about 10 times the requirement, selenium-related liver failure, vitamin A toxicity at 25 times the RDA, and polar bear liver as the classic acute vitamin A poisoning.

objectives: Describe the consequences of selenium deficiency (Keshan cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy) and excess (selenosis), and why the margin between them is narrow.
Recognise hexavalent chromium lung cancer, manganese-induced parkinsonism and prosthetic hip-associated cobalt toxicity from exposure and clinical clues.
Predict the direction of biotin interference in sandwich and competitive streptavidin immunoassays, and state the neuropathy risk of excess pyridoxine and the teratogenic risk of excess vitamin A.

scenes.title: Four patients, four exposures
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: four patient cards. (1) A welder with slow movements, stiffness and an odd gait. (2) A woman whose fractured ceramic hip was revised to a metal head, now with hearing loss and heart failure. (3) A man taking a new selenium supplement whose hair and nails are falling out and whose breath smells of garlic. (4) A woman on high-dose biotin whose thyroid results look like Graves disease. Question token: “Deficiency, toxicity, or a lab artifact?”

cues.text: Four invented patients. A welder with slow movements, stiffness and an odd gait. A woman whose broken ceramic hip was revised to a metal head, now with hearing loss and heart failure.
A man on a new selenium supplement, losing hair and nails, with garlic breath. And a woman on high-dose biotin whose thyroid results look like Graves disease.
Which is a deficiency, which is a toxicity, and which is a laboratory artifact?

scenes.title: Selenium: a narrow window
scenes.altText: Schematic seesaw for selenium. Left card “Too little”: Keshan disease, an endemic and sometimes fatal cardiomyopathy first found in Keshan County, northeast China; attributed to a combination of selenium deficiency and a mutated Coxsackie B virus strain; prolonged parenteral nutrition can cause severe deficiency with skeletal muscle pain and weakness that responds to selenium. Right card “Too much” (selenosis): hair loss, brittle or lost nails, skin rash, and a garlic odor on the breath from dimethyl selenide. Token: RDA 55–70 µg/day; US upper limit 400 µg/day; misformulated supplements gave about 22,000–32,000 µg per dose.

cues.text: Selenium has one of the narrowest gaps between deficiency and toxicity of any element. Too little is linked to Keshan disease, an endemic and sometimes fatal cardiomyopathy first found in Keshan County in northeast China.

Keshan disease is attributed to a combination of selenium deficiency and a mutated strain of Coxsackie B virus. Prolonged parenteral nutrition can also cause severe deficiency, with skeletal muscle pain and weakness that improves with selenium.
Too much causes selenosis: hair loss, brittle or lost nails, skin rash, and a garlic smell on the breath from the volatile compound dimethyl selenide.
The recommended intake is about 55 to 70 micrograms a day, with a US upper limit of 400. A misformulated supplement that delivered over 20,000 micrograms per dose caused an outbreak of selenosis.

props.label: RDA 55–70 µg/day · US upper limit 400 µg/day

scenes.title: Three metals that injure
scenes.altText: Three cards. Chromium: IARC lists chromium as a Group 1 carcinogen; trivalent chromium is largely non-toxic, while hexavalent chromium, Cr(VI), is toxic and carcinogenic; inhaled Cr(VI) raises lung cancer risk in occupational studies such as chromate production, with nasal irritation and perforation. Manganese: prolonged inhalation in mining and welding accumulates in the basal ganglia, especially the globus pallidus, causing manganism — rigidity, bradykinesia, “cock gait”, postural tremor, falling backward. Cobalt: prosthetic hip-associated cobalt toxicity — in a systematic review of 79 patients, 38 had metal-on-metal bearings and 32 had fractured ceramic bearings revised to a metal head; hearing loss 43%, visual impairment 32%, cardiomyopathy 15%, hypothyroidism or thyroid dysfunction 11%; yearly blood cobalt suggested for these bearings.

cues.text: Chromium comes in two main forms. Trivalent chromium is largely non-toxic, but hexavalent chromium, chromium six, is toxic and carcinogenic. Inhaled chromium six raises lung cancer risk in exposed workers, such as chromate production workers.

Manganese inhaled for long periods in mining and welding builds up in the basal ganglia, above all the globus pallidus. The result is manganism: rigidity, slow movement, a strutting cock gait, tremor, and falling backward. That is the welder.

Cobalt is released by worn hip implants. In a systematic review of seventy-nine patients, thirty-eight had metal-on-metal bearings, and thirty-two had broken ceramic hips revised to a metal head. That is patient two.

Hearing loss was reported in forty-three percent, visual problems in about a third, cardiomyopathy in fifteen percent and thyroid dysfunction in eleven percent. The authors suggest yearly blood cobalt checks for these bearings.

scenes.title: Megadose vitamins and the lab
scenes.altText: Four cards. Biotin, sandwich assay: excess free biotin occupies streptavidin and blocks capture → falsely LOW (for example TSH). Biotin, competitive assay: free biotin competes for streptavidin binding sites → falsely HIGH (for example cortisol); children on high-dose biotin were misdiagnosed with Graves disease (high free T4 and T3, low TSH, high TSH-receptor antibodies). Pyridoxine (B6): chronic large doses cause sensory neuropathy in a stocking-glove pattern; classic cases took > 2 g/day; US upper limit 100 mg/day, EFSA 25 mg/day; case reports near or below 25 mg/day, though controlled studies have not fully confirmed toxicity at these doses. Vitamin A: high maternal intake can be teratogenic; chronic toxicity after about 10 mg/day for months in adults; acute toxicity usually above 500 mg/day in adults (nausea, blurred vision, headache, papilledema).

cues.text: Many immunoassays link antibody to a solid phase through biotin and streptavidin. In a sandwich assay, excess biotin from a supplement occupies streptavidin and blocks capture, so results come out falsely low, for example TSH. Assays for cardiac troponin can be affected too.

In a competitive assay, for example one cortisol assay, the same excess biotin gives falsely high results. Children on high-dose biotin were misdiagnosed with Graves disease: high free T4 and T3, low TSH and high receptor antibodies. That is patient four.

Pyridoxine, vitamin B6, taken in large doses for a long time, causes a sensory neuropathy in a stocking-glove pattern. Classic cases took over two grams a day. The US upper limit is 100 milligrams a day, but Europe set 25, and case reports describe neuropathy near or below 25.

Vitamin A in excess can be teratogenic when intake in pregnancy is high. Chronic toxicity appears after about ten milligrams a day for months in adults; acute toxicity usually needs more than 500, with nausea, blurred vision, headache and papilledema.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Stop biotin overnight and retest — always enough” (✓ 8–10 h covers doses up to 10 mg/day; at least 48 h is common advice; on 300 mg/day clearance can take 73 h or longer, more with poor kidney function); “B6 neuropathy needs more than 100 mg/day” (✓ US limit 100, EFSA 25 mg/day; case reports near or below 25); “Manganism is just Parkinson disease” (✓ poor levodopa response, no Lewy bodies, more dystonia, less resting tremor).

cues.text: Trap one: stop biotin overnight and retest, that is always enough. No: eight to ten hours covers doses up to ten milligrams a day, but on 300 milligrams a day clearance can take seventy-three hours or longer, especially with poor kidney function.

Trap two: pyridoxine neuropathy only happens above 100 milligrams a day. No: Europe’s upper limit is 25, and case reports describe neuropathy near or below it, although controlled studies have not fully confirmed this.
Trap three: manganism is just Parkinson disease. No: it responds poorly to levodopa, lacks Lewy bodies, and shows more dystonia and less resting tremor.

scenes.title: Seesaw, Six and the stolen seat
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Selenium is a seesaw (heart fails at one end, hair and nails at the other); Roman numeral VI is vicious (Cr(VI) and the lungs); biotin steals streptavidin’s seat.” Tokens: Se seesaw · Cr VI = vicious · biotin steals the seat. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: selenium is a seesaw, with Keshan heart disease at one end and hair, nails and garlic breath at the other. Roman numeral six is vicious: chromium six and the lungs. And biotin steals streptavidin’s seat.

Where it breaks: Keshan disease also involves a virus, not selenium alone; trivalent chromium has also been reported as potentially toxic; and a stolen seat gives falsely low sandwich results but falsely high competitive ones.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Selenium: Keshan heart ↔ selenosis · chromium six → lung cancer · manganese → pallidal parkinsonism · hip cobalt → hearing, vision, heart”, “Biotin: sandwich low, competitive high · B6 → sensory neuropathy · vitamin A → teratogen”.

cues.text: Selenium has a narrow window between Keshan cardiomyopathy and selenosis, inhaled hexavalent chromium raises lung cancer risk, manganese causes a parkinsonism that resists levodopa and hip-implant cobalt harms hearing, vision and the heart, while megadose biotin distorts streptavidin immunoassays in either direction and excess pyridoxine and vitamin A cause neuropathy and birth defects.

Biotin: sandwich low, competitive high · B6 → neuropathy · vitamin A → teratogen

explanation.what: Plain language: some trace elements and vitamins are harmful when too low, others when too high, and one vitamin, biotin, mainly causes trouble by fooling laboratory tests. Scientific terms: Keshan disease, Coxsackie B virus, selenosis, dimethyl selenide, glutathione peroxidase, trivalent and hexavalent chromium, IARC Group 1, manganism, globus pallidus, levodopa, Lewy bodies, prosthetic hip-associated cobalt toxicity (PHACT), metal-on-metal bearing, streptavidin–biotin immunoassay, sandwich and competitive formats, biotin washout, pyridoxine, tolerable upper intake level, retinol, hypervitaminosis A.
explanation.why: Selenium is built into selenoproteins with roles in heart and skeletal muscle function, so deficiency is linked to muscle disorders, while excess causes selenosis. Hexavalent chromium is the toxic, carcinogenic form, especially when inhaled. Manganese accumulates most in the globus pallidus, whose neurons appear most sensitive to manganese-induced degeneration; links to disturbed dopamine signalling are reported but not settled. Worn or abraded hip bearings release cobalt into blood. Free biotin occupies streptavidin binding sites, so the assay cannot capture its biotinylated reagent.
explanation.measure: Selenium: low glutathione peroxidase activity indicates low selenium status; nail selenium tracked exposure in a supplement outbreak. Manganese: raised blood and urine manganese and T1 MRI hyperintensity of the globus pallidus support exposure. Cobalt: blood cobalt, with yearly checks suggested for metal-on-metal or revised fractured ceramic bearings. Biotin: suspect when results clash with the clinical picture; retest after an adequate washout (8–10 h for up to 10 mg/day; much longer at 300 mg/day or with poor kidney function) or on a non-streptavidin method. Vitamin A: plasma retinol above 2.09 µmol/L defines hypervitaminosis.
explanation.differs: Cr(III) (largely non-toxic) vs Cr(VI) (carcinogen); manganism (poor levodopa response, no Lewy bodies, more dystonia, less resting tremor) vs Parkinson disease; biotin in sandwich assays (falsely low) vs competitive assays (falsely high).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: Keshan disease and selenosis signs, which chromium form is carcinogenic, the welder with parkinsonism, a hip implant with hearing loss and cardiomyopathy, a Graves-like thyroid panel on biotin, falsely low troponin on biotin, and the neuropathy of pyridoxine megadoses.

mnemonic.text: Seesaw, Six and the stolen seat: selenium is a seesaw (Keshan heart at one end, hair, nails and garlic breath at the other); Roman numeral VI is vicious (chromium VI and the lungs); biotin steals streptavidin’s seat.
mnemonic.explanation: Links selenium’s narrow window, the carcinogenic chromium form and the mechanism of biotin interference to three short images.
mnemonic.limitation: Keshan disease also involves a Coxsackie B virus co-factor, not selenium alone; trivalent chromium has also been reported as potentially toxic; and the stolen seat gives falsely low sandwich results but falsely high competitive results.

The seesaw ignores the viral co-factor in Keshan disease and individual differences in selenium tolerance.
takeaway: Selenium has a narrow window between Keshan cardiomyopathy and selenosis, inhaled hexavalent chromium raises lung cancer risk, manganese causes a parkinsonism that resists levodopa and hip-implant cobalt harms hearing, vision and the heart, while megadose biotin distorts streptavidin immunoassays in either direction and excess pyridoxine and vitamin A cause neuropathy and birth defects.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman taking 300 mg/day of biotin has high free T4, low TSH and a positive TSH-receptor antibody on streptavidin–biotin immunoassays, but no symptoms of hyperthyroidism. What is the best next step?

options.text: Suspect biotin interference; retest after a washout of days, or on a method that does not use streptavidin–biotin
options.rationale: Correct. Excess biotin gives falsely high competitive results and falsely low sandwich results, a pattern that mimicked Graves disease in children on high-dose biotin; at 300 mg/day washout can take 73 h or longer.

options.text: Diagnose Graves disease and start antithyroid treatment
options.rationale: Incorrect. The results clash with the clinical picture and fit the known Graves-like biotin artifact.

options.text: Retest the next morning after stopping biotin overnight
options.rationale: Incorrect. An 8–10 h washout covers doses up to 10 mg/day; at 300 mg/day biotin can persist for 73 h or longer.

options.text: Repeat on the same assay with a heterophile blocking tube
options.rationale: Incorrect. The likely cause is free biotin competing at the streptavidin–biotin step; the approaches described are an adequate washout, removing biotin with streptavidin-coated particles, or a method without streptavidin–biotin chemistry.

questions.stem: Two years after a fractured ceramic hip was revised to a metal head, a 62-year-old develops hearing loss, blurred vision and new cardiomyopathy. Which test is most useful?

options.rationale: Correct. Revision of a fractured ceramic bearing to a metal head is one of the two most common settings described for prosthetic hip-associated cobalt toxicity, whose reported features include hearing and visual loss and cardiomyopathy.
Incorrect. Selenium deficiency can cause cardiomyopathy, but the implant history and hearing and visual loss point to cobalt.
Incorrect. Manganese toxicity presents as parkinsonism after inhalation exposure, not as hearing loss and cardiomyopathy after a hip revision.

options.text: None, because only metal-on-metal bearings release cobalt
options.rationale: Incorrect. In a systematic review, 32 of 79 cases followed revision of a fractured ceramic bearing to a metal head.

questions.stem: A long-time welder has rigidity, slow movements, a strutting gait and falls when stepping backward. Levodopa gives no benefit, and T1-weighted MRI shows bright globus pallidus signal. Which is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. Manganese from welding fumes accumulates in the globus pallidus; manganism responds poorly to levodopa.
Incorrect. Parkinson disease usually responds to levodopa and shows Lewy bodies; the exposure and pallidal MRI signal point to manganese.
Incorrect. Inhaled chromium VI is linked to lung cancer and nasal injury; the welding exposure, levodopa failure and pallidal MRI signal point to manganese.
Incorrect. Selenium deficiency is linked to cardiomyopathy and skeletal muscle disorders; the exposure and MRI findings here point to manganese.

claims.text: Keshan disease: endemic, sometimes fatal cardiomyopathy first found in Keshan County, northeast China; attributed to selenium deficiency combined with a mutated Coxsackie B virus strain.
Prolonged parenteral nutrition can cause severe selenium deficiency with skeletal muscle pain and weakness responding to selenium.
Selenosis: hair loss, nail damage, skin rash, garlic breath (dimethyl selenide); narrow margin; RDA 55–70 µg/day, US upper limit 400 µg/day; misformulated supplement outbreak.
Chromium IARC Group 1; Cr(III) largely non-toxic but reported as potentially toxic; Cr(VI) toxic and carcinogenic; inhaled Cr(VI) and occupational lung cancer risk; nasal injury.
Manganism from inhalation in mining and welding; globus pallidus; clinical features; distinguished from Parkinson disease by levodopa response, Lewy bodies, dystonia and tremor.
Prosthetic hip-associated cobalt toxicity: bearing types, symptom frequencies, yearly blood cobalt.
Biotin interference: falsely low sandwich and falsely high competitive results; Graves-like misdiagnosis; washout depends on dose and renal function.
Pyridoxine sensory neuropathy; classic doses above 2 g/day; US UL 100 vs EFSA UL 25 mg/day; case reports near or below 25 mg/day, not fully confirmed by controlled studies.
Vitamin A: teratogenic at high maternal intake; chronic toxicity after 10 mg/day for months; acute above 500 mg/day in adults; acute symptoms; plasma retinol above 2.09 µM.

Reviewer details not taught: selenium toxic at about 10 times the requirement, selenium-related liver failure, vitamin A toxic at 25 times the RDA, polar bear liver as classic acute vitamin A toxicity.
claims.note: Not taught as facts in this lesson; not verified against an external source read here.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 27 Hit 14 ties pyridoxine neuropathy to more than 100 mg/day. Hadtstein 2021 notes the US upper limit is 100 mg/day but EFSA set 25 mg/day, and case reports describe neuropathy at doses near or below 25 mg/day, suggesting wide individual differences, although the authors caution that controlled studies may not fully support toxicity at these lower doses (register flag rv-b6-neuropathy-dose-threshold).

Ch. 27 Hit 11 links cobalt toxicity to metal-on-metal hips only. Crutsen 2022 found 32 of 79 cases after revision of a fractured ceramic bearing to a metal head (38 metal-on-metal), with higher mean blood cobalt in the revised ceramic group (register flag rv-cobalt-hip-revised-ceramic).

Ch. 27 Hit 11 says manganism mimics Parkinson disease. Kwakye 2015 describes it as distinguishable: no Lewy bodies, lack of levodopa response, more dystonia and less resting tremor, with globus pallidus accumulation (register flag rv-manganism-distinguishable-pd).

Ch. 27 Hit 14 says to hold biotin before testing without duration or error direction. Luong 2020 gives 8–10 h for up to 10 mg/day, common advice of at least 48 h, and up to 73 h or longer at 300 mg/day or with poor renal function, and notes falsely low sandwich but falsely high competitive results (register flag rv-biotin-washout-direction-ch27).
